## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, resume-research.
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.

1	# Research standards
2	
3	The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.
4	
5	## 1. Evidence labels
6	Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:
7	
8	| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
9	|---|---|---|---|
10	| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
11	| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
12	| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |
13	
14	Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.
15	
16	Citation syntax:
17	- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
18	- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
19	- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.
20	
21	## 2. Never invent
22	- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
23	- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
24	- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
25	- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.
26	
27	## 3. Source quality tiers
28	Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.
29	
30	1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
31	2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
32	3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
33	4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
34	5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.
35	
36	`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
37	Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.
38	
39	## 4. Reading depth
40	- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
41	- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
42	- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".
43	
44	## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
45	For every empirical paper check and record:
46	- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
47	- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
48	- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
49	- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
50	- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
51	- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
52	- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).
53	
54	Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.
55	
56	## 6. Contradictions
57	When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.
58	
59	## 7. Research gaps and novelty
60	A gap is reported only when:
61	1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
62	2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
63	3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".
64	
65	## 8. Copyright and access
66	- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
67	- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
68	- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
69	- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.
70	
71	## 9. Preservation
72	- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
73	- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
74	- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
75	- `research-log.md` is append-only.
76	
77	## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
78	- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
79	- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
80	- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
81	- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.
82	---
83	name: analyze-paper
84	description: Analyse one research paper in depth (objective, method, data, setup, metrics, findings, limitations, validity threats, future work, relevance) with page-cited evidence. Use when a project paper needs its analysis.md written or completed.
85	---
86	
87	# Analyse a paper
88	
89	`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) — labels §1, never invent §2, reading depth §4, appraisal checklist §5.
90	
91	Input: project id + paper key. Files live in `research/<id>/papers/<key>/`.
92	
93	## 1. Prepare
94	- `rlab scaffold <id> <key>` (creates `analysis.md`; never overwrites an existing one).
95	- Read `metadata.json`. Note `venue_kind`, `is_retracted`, `fulltext.status`, `fulltext.identity`, `fulltext.text_layer`.
96	- `identity` UNCONFIRMED → read PDF page 1 and confirm it is this paper; if not, stop and report.
97	- `text_layer` POOR → read pages from `paper.pdf` with the Read tool (`pages` parameter) instead of `fulltext.txt`.
98	- No full text → `evidence_basis: abstract-only`; fill objective and headline claims as [A] from the abstract in `metadata.json`, write "full text not available" in sections 3–6, 8 and 10, and stop at step 4.
99	
100	## 2. Read the whole paper
101	Read `fulltext.txt` in chunks (Read with offset/limit) from start to end: abstract, introduction, method, results, tables, discussion, limitations, conclusion. Use Grep for `limitation|threat|future work|we did not|sample|dataset|N =` to make sure nothing is missed. For tables or figures garbled by text extraction, read that PDF page directly. Page numbers come from the nearest preceding `=== [PDF page N] ===` marker.
102	
103	## 3. Write the analysis
104	Fill every section of `analysis.md`. Each [V]/[A] item ends with `(p. N)`. Use "not reported" when the paper is silent — that absence is itself useful information (e.g. no sample size reported). Separate author-stated limitations (section 8, [A]) from limitations you identify (section 9, [I]). Apply the appraisal checklist to section 10. Fill the evidence table (section 13) with rows linked to project RQ ids from `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.
105	
106	## 4. Frontmatter
107	Fill the single-line frontmatter fields: `design`, `dataset`, `sample_size`, `metrics`, `main_finding` (≤25 words), `relevance` (high/medium/low). These feed the literature matrix.
108	
109	## 5. Self-check
110	- Every [V]/[A] has a page ref; `rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/papers/<key>/analysis.md` passes.
111	- Grep `fulltext.txt` for 3 of your quotes/numbers: each is found on the cited page.
112	- No template placeholder or empty required section remains.
113	Then set `status: ready` and run `rlab index <id>`.
114	
115	Done when: `status: ready` and the self-check passed — or `status: draft` with the blocking reason written in "Analyst notes".
116	
117	## 6. Return
118	Report: key, 2-line summary, evidence-table rows, anything surprising (contradicts other work, suspicious results, missing data).
119	# Critical review: analyses batch B (2026-11-11)
120	
121	Scope: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` for 10 keys, checked against `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index) and `metadata.json`.
122	Reviewer role: sceptical peer review. No analysis file was edited.
123	
124	## Checks run
125	
126	- `rlab cite-check 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding <10 analysis files>`: **OK** (59–89 citations per file, all to the paper's own key).
127	- `rlab validate <id> <key>`: **could not run.** It fails with `pdftotext not found` (poppler is not installed on this machine). As a fallback I read the `metadata.json` fields:
128	  - all 10 papers have `verification.status = verified` and `is_retracted = false`;
129	  - PDF identity is `match (arXiv id printed in PDF)` for 8 papers;
130	  - PDF identity is only `probable (title found on first pages)` for si2025benchmarking and wu2026looks. Both are ACL Anthology PDFs, and title, authors and venue footer agree with the metadata.
131	  - The DOI `10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650` (wu2026looks) looks malformed because it has no `v1/`, but it resolves at doi.org (302 to aclanthology.org). The `v1/` variant gives 404. **No problem.**
132	  - **Action:** install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` for all 10 keys before setting any of them to `complete`.
133	- Spot checks: for each paper I grepped at least 5 numbers or claims (all Key-findings numbers, the sample size and the dataset) in `fulltext.txt` and checked the cited page. Most were correct. The deviations are listed below.
134	- RQ links: every analysis cites RQ1–RQ5, and all five exist in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.
135	
136	## Summary
137	
138	| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
139	|---|---|---|
140	| mota2026comparing | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
141	| pan2026functional | pass-with-minor-fixes | 4 |
142	| si2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
143	| tran2026vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 6 |
144	| wu2026looks | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
145	| xiao2025benchmarking | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
146	| yang2026programbench | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
147	| zhao2025vibe | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
148	| zhou2025declarui | pass-with-minor-fixes | 2 |
149	| zhu2026understanding | pass-with-minor-fixes | 3 |
150	
151	Overall quality is high:
152	- All 10 are full-text analyses with dense, mostly correct page refs.
153	- Their own critiques are paper-specific, not boilerplate (e.g. the DeclarUI ablation arithmetic, the MobileForge screenshot-only contradiction, the RAL-Bench contamination evidence).
154	- No invented numbers were found.
155	
156	The errors are mostly mislabelled author claims, a few factual slips in evidence-table rows (these feed the evidence matrix), and version/provenance drift.
157	
158	---
159	
160	## mota2026comparing — pass-with-minor-fixes
161	
162	1. **§9 bullet 1.**
163	   - Current: "a single outlier project (Lovable's wildlife-whisperer-app, p. 3) changes the tool ranking on issues and effort."
164	   - Problem: only half true. Replace the outlier's 59 issues with a value like its siblings (~165) and Lovable's raw issue total rises to ~496, above Replit's 463. The effort ranking does not change: each of the other two Lovable projects alone (1,782 and 1,774 min) exceeds v0's three-project total (941 min) (Table 3, p. 3; Table 6, p. 5).
165	   - Correct: "…changes the raw issue-count ranking (Lovable would exceed Replit), but not the remediation-effort ranking (p. 3, p. 5)."
166	2. **§9 bullet 4.**
167	   - Current: "the 'highest remediation effort' conclusion rests on a narrow base."
168	   - Problem: overstated, for the reason given in fix 1. The narrow part is the rule concentration (S1874, p. 6), not the project base.
169	   - Correct: "Lovable's effort lead is robust across 2 of 3 projects (p. 3) but is driven mainly by one rule, S1874, which per the authors accounts for more than half of the effort (p. 6); whether that rule reflects template code is unknown."
170	3. **§7 finding 3, label.**
171	   - Problem: "…and, per the authors, more than half of Lovable's effort (p. 6)" sits inside a [V] item. This share cannot be derived from any table; it is an author statement.
172	   - Fix: split it out as "[A] S1874 accounts for more than half of Lovable's remediation effort (p. 6)."
173	
174	## pan2026functional — pass-with-minor-fixes
175	
176	1. **§13 evidence row RQ3 (factual error).**
177	   - Current: "Reference-normalised maintainability (MI lower bound) averages ~31–33%, the weakest non-functional dimension."
178	   - Problem: Resource is lower than Maintainability in both tables: standard LLMs Res 31.25 vs Maint 33.45; thinking LLMs Res 28.92 vs Maint 31.38 (Tables 4–5, p. 6).
179	   - Correct: "…averages 33.45% (standard) and 31.38% (thinking), among the two weakest dimensions with resource usage (31.25% / 28.92%), while security averages 87.40% / 85.32% (p. 6)."
180	   - This row feeds the evidence matrix, so fix it before synthesis.
181	2. **§9 last-but-one bullet.**
182	   - Current: "All projects are Python libraries or CLI-style tools (p. 2), with no GUI, web front end or interactive application."
183	   - Problem: Table 1 includes mitmproxy (which has a web interface), Mailpile (a webmail client), glances and folium (web maps) (p. 2). The accurate limit is how they are tested, not what they are.
184	   - Correct: "All 38 projects are Python and are evaluated only through black-box pytest suites against their Python API/CLI surface (p. 3–4); UI behaviour is never exercised."
185	3. **§9 prompt-sensitivity bullet.**

The Analyst notes flag this, but the numbers that look broken (ablation Table 2) may have been corrected in the published version. PACMSE is an ACM open-access journal, so a legal published copy is probably available.
304	   - Fix: try `rlab fetch` for the ACM version, re-check Tables 1–3, and record any differences in a Revision section.

326	## Cross-paper observations
327	
328	1. **Same-family construction or judging, with same-family winners (a recurring threat).**
329	   - ProgramBench: tests were written by Claude Sonnet 4.5 with source access, and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 3; p. 31].

331	   - MobileForge: Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and candidate [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
332	   - SusVibes: the environment builder is Claude 4 Sonnet, and SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet is best on FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7; p. 17].
333	   - Only MobileForge tests self-preference, and only qualitatively [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
334	   - The evidence matrix should list this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not repeat it per paper.
335	2. **Does iterative feedback help? There is an apparent tension.**
336	   - One-shot self-repair, environment repair and planning did not raise functional scores and lowered non-functional quality [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
337	   - Browser self-testing correlates with accuracy (r = 0.72 across 16 models) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
338	   - Compiler-feedback loops raise compile success, 74% to 98% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9], and make build success saturate at 100% [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
339	   - [I] Possible reconciliation: one-shot interventions vs multi-step agentic loops, and different outcome metrics (non-functional quality vs workflow pass / compilation). Record both sides under "Contradictions" in the evidence matrix (standards §6). Do not pick a side.
340	3. **Reasoning or "thinking" effort.**
341	   - "Thinking" models are not consistently better and average slightly below standard ones [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
342	   - Higher reasoning effort clearly helps GPT and Gemini 3.1 Pro on Vibe Code Bench (20-app subset) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
343	   - These differ in setting (single pass vs agentic) and are not a direct contradiction, but should be noted.

345	   - Rebuilt CLIs are smaller and more monolithic than the human originals [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
346	   - Among models, the visual leader writes 2.2× more code with larger files [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
347	   - Replit produces about 60% duplicated lines [@mota2026comparing, p. 4].
348	   - MetaGPT needed explicit modularity prompts to avoid monolithic God classes [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
349	   - "More code is worse" is not established. Both mota (per KLOC) and zhu (raw counts, ρ = 0.94 with TLoC) treat smell counts as size-driven, but only mota normalises.

351	   - zhu2026understanding argues that SonarQube issue counts conflate linting with structural smells, and positions itself against Santa Molison et al. (= project key `molison2025llm`) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2].
352	   - mota2026comparing relies on SonarQube alone [@mota2026comparing, p. 2].
353	   - When synthesising RQ3, check molison2025llm's analysis for this disagreement about measurement validity.
354	6. **Possible data overlap.**
355	   - Interaction2Code takes 100 of its 127 pages from the C4 validation set, using Design2Code's filtering [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2].
356	   - Design2Code's 484 pages also come from the C4 validation set [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2].
357	   - The two benchmarks may share source pages, so they are not fully independent evidence on screenshot-to-code fidelity.
358	   - Both reuse the same Position metric (1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|)) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
359	7. **Version drift.**
360	   - Four analyses cite a published DOI but analyse an arXiv version: tran2026vibe (v3), xiao2025benchmarking (v3, later than ASE 2025), zhou2025declarui (v1, earlier than PACMSE), zhu2026understanding (v1, with a different title).
361	   - zhao2025vibe has the opposite problem: published, but metadata says preprint.
362	   - Page refs follow the arXiv PDFs in all four cases, so quotes in reports must cite the PDF actually held.
363	8. **Model overlap allows a weak consistency check.**
364	   - Claude Opus 4.6 is top-tier in three independent benchmarks [@tran2026vibe, p. 6; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @wu2026looks, p. 7].
365	   - GPT-5.2 appears in pan (41.81% functional) and tran (53.50%), and is also the worst-aligned judge in tran [@pan2026functional, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 9].
366	   - [I] Rankings agree in broad terms, but the metrics are not comparable, so absolute numbers must not be pooled.
367	9. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
368	   - Only Interaction2Code runs an explicit check, a BLEU similarity to the original HTML [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], and the analysis rightly calls it weak.
369	   - ProgramBench uses a different-language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
370	   - RAL-Bench acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
371	   - MobileForge, DeclarUI, SusVibes and Design2Code do not discuss contamination of their own data, even though all use popular public apps or pages.
372	   - This is a candidate RQ4/RQ5 gap and needs a novelty check before it can be claimed.

19	    18	# Interaction2Code: Benchmarking MLLM-based Interactive Webpage Code Generation from Interactive Prototyping
20	    19	
21	    20	- Authors: Xiao, Jingyu; Wan, Yuxuan; Huo, Yintong; Wang, Zixin; Xu, Xinyi; Wang, Wenxuan
22	    21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) (published)
23	    22	- DOI: 10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028
24	    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
25	    24	
26	    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
28	    27	
29	    28	## 1. Research objective
30	    29	- Formulate the Interaction-to-Code task (generate an interactive webpage from an "interactive prototype": screenshots before and after each interaction), build a real-world benchmark for it, and systematically study how well MLLMs reproduce webpage interactions, why they fail, and how prompting can help [A] (pp. 1–2).
31	    30	
32	    31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	    32	- No formal RQs. The study is organised around four reported "limitations" of MLLMs: (1) worse generation of interactive parts than of the full page; (2) ten failure types; (3) poor performance on visually subtle interactions; (4) insufficient understanding from visual input alone — each paired with an improvement strategy [V] (pp. 1–2).
34	    33	
35	    34	## 3. Methodology
36	    35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus empirical comparison of models and prompts; automatic evaluation via Selenium-driven interaction replay; human usability and pairwise evaluation; qualitative failure taxonomy; sub-experiments on visual saliency and input modality; ablation; small user study [V] (pp. 3–11).
37	    36	- Approach / model / intervention: MLLM receives the original screenshot plus post-interaction screenshot(s) and must output one HTML+CSS+JavaScript file, tagging interactive elements with ids (e.g. id="interact1") so a webdriver can trigger them [V] (pp. 3–5). Prompts: Direct, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Mark (red bounding boxes on interactive areas), Failure-aware Prompt (FAP: lists the ten failure types) [V] (p. 5). Further enhancements: Visual Saliency Enhancement (crop to enlarge the interaction area) and adding human-written textual descriptions of interactions [V] (pp. 9–10).
38	    37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o-20240806, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620, Qwen2.5-VL-instruct 3B/7B/72B; Direct prompting is the baseline for prompt comparisons; Gemini-1.5-flash Direct is the human pairwise baseline [V] (pp. 4, 6). No non-LLM or prior UI-to-code system (e.g. DCGen) is run as a baseline [I] (based on p. 4 model list).
39	    38	
40	    39	## 4. Dataset and sample
41	    40	- Data source(s): (1) C4 validation set (CommonCrawl), filtered as in Design2Code, 1,000 pages sampled across 15 topics, from which four PhD students each picked about 25 → 100 pages; (2) 27 popular GitHub projects (average 13k stars) with deployed links, found via "open-production-web-projects" and "awesome-opensource-apps", to include UI-framework pages [V] (pp. 2–3).
42	    41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 127 webpages and 374 interactions; 15+ topics; 23 tag categories and 8 visual categories (31 interaction categories) [V] (pp. 1, 3). Most frequent interactive tags: button 235, input 52, span 37, link 36 [V] (p. 3).
43	    42	- Sampling / selection method: manual selection by four PhD students for complexity (at least one meaningful interaction) and diversity; 1–10 "important and functional" interactions kept per page; trivial interactions (e.g. hover underline) excluded [V] (pp. 2–3). Selection guidelines are only in the external artifact [V] (p. 3).
44	    43	- Data availability (public? link?): data and code at https://github.com/WebPAI/Interaction2Code [A] (p. 1).
45	    44	
46	    45	## 5. Experimental setup
47	    46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: temperature 0; max output 4,096 tokens (commercial) and 2,048 (Qwen); other parameters default [V] (p. 4). Selenium webdriver locates elements by id, performs the interaction and screenshots the result; the changed region is extracted by pixel subtraction (same-size pages) or a Git-diff of rows/columns (size-changing pages) (Algorithm 1) [V] (p. 4). Data-contamination check: BLEU between generated and original HTML is 0.12–0.14 for the four main models [V] (p. 5). FAP experiment: 2/3 of the dataset used to derive failure types, 1/3 for testing [V] (p. 8). Saliency and modality experiments use 10 randomly sampled failure-case webpages each [V] (pp. 9–10).
48	    47	- Code availability: GitHub repository above [A] (p. 1). Appendix H (tool) and detailed human-evaluation instructions are referenced but are not in our 13-page PDF [V] (pp. 6, 11).
49	    48	
50	    49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
51	    50	- Full-page metrics: CLIP score (visual similarity); SSIM (structural similarity); Text similarity = BLEU on OCR-extracted text; Widget Similarity (WS) and Widget Match Rate (WMR) computed with the GUIPilot method [V] (p. 4).
52	    51	- Interaction-part metrics (on the extracted changed region): CLIP, SSIM, Text; Position similarity P = 1 − max(|xo − xg|, |yo − yg|) of normalised interaction-area centres; Implement Rate IR = implemented / (implemented + unimplemented), where "implemented" means detectable by the webdriver [V] (p. 4).
53	    52	- Human metrics: Usability Rate UR = usable / (usable + unusable), judged by four PhD students (three years front-end experience) — usable if the implementation "precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype"; pairwise Win/Tie/Lose by five annotators against Gemini-1.5-flash Direct, majority (≥3) rule; failure-type annotation [V] (pp. 4, 6–7).
54	    53	- Validation against human judgement: authors state human results "are consistent with Section V-A, confirming the validity of our automatic evaluation metrics" [A] (p. 6). No correlation coefficient, agreement statistic or regression is reported — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement for usability, pairwise or failure annotation — not reported (failure types reached by discussion to consensus on a 25% sample) [V] (p. 7). Number of items in the human evaluations — not reported.
55	    54	- Widget metrics are acknowledged as unreliable for web pages: WS is "consistently poor" (0.02–0.05) and GUIPilot omits many elements because it was designed for mobile UIs [V] (pp. 5–6).
56	    55	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none for model or prompt comparisons; saliency effect described as "significantly increases" without a test [V] (pp. 8–9). Not reported.
57	    56	
58	    57	## 7. Key findings
59	    58	1. Interactive parts are generated worse than full pages for all models (e.g. GPT-4o average full-page CLIP 0.7059 vs interaction-part CLIP 0.5598) [V] (p. 6).
60	    59	2. Claude-3.5-Sonnet has the best averages on most metrics (e.g. interaction IR 0.7870, full-page Text 0.5835); GPT-4o with Mark prompt has the highest single IR (0.8128); Qwen2.5-VL-72B ≈ Gemini-1.5-flash; performance rises with model size [V] (pp. 5–6).
61	    60	3. Human Usability Rate (Fig. 6a, read from figure labels): GPT-4o Direct/CoT/Mark 73/74/81%; Claude 66/69/77%; Gemini 47/53/64%; Qwen-72B 41/43/54%; Qwen-3B 17–19% [V] (p. 6). Mark prompting gives the largest usability gain (Claude +11 points vs Direct) [V] (p. 6).
62	    61	4. Ten failure types in two groups (interactive element: missing, no interaction, wrong element, wrong type, wrong position; interaction effects: wrong position, wrong type, effect on wrong element, partial implementation, wrong function) [V] (pp. 7–8). Failures (a) missing element, (b) no interaction and (j) wrong function have usability <10% (0%, 6.93%, 0%) [V] (pp. 7–8). Main failure modes are "No interaction", "Partial implementation", "Interactive element missing" and "Wrong function" [A] (p. 8).
63	    62	5. Failures cluster into spatial (a, c, e, f), type (d, g) and behavioural (b, h, i, j) failures [A] (p. 8).
64	    63	6. Low visual saliency (small interaction area) lowers SSIM and position similarity; cropping to enlarge the area (1.2–3×) recovers interactions on 10 failure pages [V] (pp. 9–10).
65	    64	7. On 10 failure pages, combining visual and human-written text descriptions beats either modality alone for GPT-4o (Direct: Position 0.7157 V+T vs 0.3951 V) [V] (p. 10). All four enhancements combined give the best ablation result (GPT-4o interaction CLIP 0.6937 vs 0.5700) [V] (p. 11).
66	    65	8. FAP: authors claim it improves "all models" [A] (p. 8), but Table VI shows Qwen2.5-VL-3B drops on 7 of 8 metrics and Qwen-7B on 5 of 8 [V] (p. 9).
67	    66	9. User study: with the tool, 4 tasks took 279 s vs 413 s on average and expert similarity rating 4.5 vs 3.875 (two participants per condition, two raters) [V] (p. 11).
68	    67	10. Code quality or maintainability of the generated HTML/CSS/JS is not measured; the only code-level measure is BLEU against the original HTML, used as a contamination check [V] (pp. 4–5).
69	    68	
70	    69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
71	    70	- Limited context length: complex pages with many interactions may exceed the context window; iterative generation suggested [A] (p. 11).
72	    71	- Model selection: only three main commercial MLLMs tested; others (e.g. Pixtral) left for future work [A] (p. 11).
73	    72	- Back-end interactions (login, search) cannot be evaluated because the benchmark has no back-end code [A] (p. 11).
74	    73	- Existing widget-consistency methods are designed for mobile UIs and miss web elements [A] (p. 5).
75	    74	
76	    75	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	    76	- [I] Validation of automatic metrics against humans is only a qualitative "consistent" statement (p. 6); no correlation, agreement (kappa) or item counts are given. The automatic metrics are therefore not shown to measure functional fidelity.
78	    77	- [I] "Implement Rate" counts an interaction as implemented if the webdriver can find and trigger the element (p. 4) — this measures presence, not correct behaviour; functional correctness rests on the human Usability Rate alone.
79	    78	- [I] Interaction fidelity is judged on screenshots of state changes, not on behavioural traces or DOM/state assertions; non-visual effects (data, network, storage) are out of scope (based on pp. 3–4, 11).
80	    79	- [I] Several sub-experiments use only 10 pages (pp. 9–10) and the user study has 2 participants per condition (p. 11); these results are anecdotal.
81	    80	- [I] The FAP claim ("improve ... on all models", p. 8) contradicts the paper's own Table VI (p. 9) for the two smaller Qwen models.
82	    81	- [I] The FAP test uses failure types derived from 2/3 of the same dataset (p. 8); split procedure and whether it is by page or by interaction is not stated.
83	    82	- [I] Fig. 9 "No failure" shares (about 36% for GPT-4o, about 40% for Claude, read from the figure, p. 9) look hard to reconcile with Usability Rates of 73–81% (p. 6); the denominators/definitions are not explained.
84	    83	- [I] The contamination argument (C4 has only text; BLEU 0.12–0.14, p. 5) is weak: C4 URLs' HTML is widely crawled elsewhere, and low BLEU does not rule out memorised layout.
85	    84	- [I] No code-quality, maintainability or code-structure measurement, despite generating JavaScript event logic.
86	    85	
87	    86	## 10. Threats to validity
88	    87	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): pages and interactions hand-picked by the authors' annotators (pp. 2–3); FAP failure types derived from the same benchmark (p. 8); Table VI direct baselines differ from Table IV (different subset), so improvements are relative to a subset [I].
89	    88	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 127 pages, front-end only, no back-end; mostly click-type interactions on buttons (235 of tagged elements) (p. 3); single-file output, not multi-file framework projects [I].
90	    89	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): visual metrics on changed regions approximate interaction fidelity; IR measures element presence; widget metrics admitted unreliable for web (p. 5) [I].
91	    90	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single deterministic run (temperature 0); no tests, CIs or agreement statistics; small N in sub-studies [I].
92	    91	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and code released (p. 1); prompts shown (p. 5); key guidelines and appendix only in the artifact; the PDF is arXiv v3 (1 Mar 2026), the ASE 2025 version may differ [I].
93	    92	
94	    93	## 11. Future research directions
95	    94	- Stated by authors [A]: iterative multi-round generation for many interactions; testing more MLLMs (e.g. Pixtral) (p. 11); handling interactions that require back-end code (p. 11); designing widget-level consistency detection suited to web pages (pp. 5–6).
96	    95	- Suggested by us [I]: validate interaction metrics against human usability with reported correlations; add behavioural assertions (DOM state, event sequences) and code-quality/maintainability analysis of generated JS; extend to multi-page apps with back-end.
97	    96	
98	    97	## 12. Relevance to our research
99	    98	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
100	    99	- How it informs our work [I]: this is the closest web benchmark to reverse engineering from observable behaviour: input is before/after screenshots of interactions, and the target is a page that reproduces that behaviour. It supplies a usable failure taxonomy and the Usability Rate as a human functional-fidelity measure, but its automatic metrics are weakly validated and it ignores code quality.

152	    27	
153	    28	## 1. Research objective
154	    29	- [A] Measure whether software-engineering (SWE) agents can develop whole programs "holistically", including the high-level architecture decisions that existing bug-fix or single-feature benchmarks do not test (p. 1; p. 2).
155	    30	- [A] Task: "given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable's behavior" (p. 1).
156	    31	
157	    32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
158	    33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [I] Implicit questions: (1) can LMs rebuild real programs from an executable plus docs; (2) do generated behavioural tests capture the programs well enough to judge this; (3) how do model-written codebases and development trajectories differ from human ones; (4) how often do models cheat when allowed internet access.
159	    34	
160	    35	## 3. Methodology
161	    36	- Research design: [V] A benchmark built semi-automatically from open-source repositories, plus an evaluation of 9 LMs, two ablations (forced different language; internet access with cheating detection), test-suite validation (coverage, assertion strength) and descriptive analyses of codebases and trajectories (p. 3; p. 5; p. 7; p. 9).
162	    37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] The agent receives the compiled gold executable (execute-only permissions, so it cannot be decompiled) and its usage documentation, inside a Docker container without internet. It must write source code in any language plus a build script that produces an executable with the same behaviour (p. 2; p. 4; p. 18). [V] The system prompt forbids obtaining source code, wrapping the binary, and decompiling or tracing it (strace/ltrace); only running the executable and reading the bundled docs is allowed (p. 19; p. 20).
163	    38	- Fidelity oracle: [V] Behavioural tests are generated by a SWE-agent (mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5) that explores the program, its source code, existing tests and documentation. It harvests existing behavioural tests and iteratively adds tests that cover missing code paths, guided by line coverage (p. 3). Assertions target observable effects only: stdout/stderr content, exit codes and files produced (p. 2; p. 3). Weak tests are flagged by an assertion-quality linter and revised. Tests that do not pass the gold binary deterministically, or that pass a dummy binary, are discarded (p. 3; p. 27). The tests are never shown to the solving agent (p. 3).
164	    39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 LMs compared with each other; no human baseline ("we do not carry out any formal human studies") (p. 5; p. 20). For test quality, the generated suites are compared with the projects' native test suites (p. 7; p. 8).
165	    40	- [I] Relation to our topic: this is the closest design to black-box reverse engineering of an application. The agent observes the running program and its docs but not the source, and fidelity is judged by behavioural equivalence. The targets are CLI/TUI programs, not GUI or web apps.
166	    41	
167	    42	## 4. Dataset and sample
168	    43	- Data source(s): [V] 200 GitHub repositories in compiled languages that build a standalone executable: Rust 107, Go 46, C/C++ 45, other 2 (one Java, one Haskell). They range from small CLI tools to FFmpeg, SQLite, DuckDB, PHP and Lua (p. 2; p. 4).
169	    44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 200 tasks; 248,853 test functions (median 770 per task, min 224, max 14,645) (p. 4). [V] 9 models x 200 tasks = 1,800 runs (p. 10); some analyses use 1,788 runs (p. 32). [V] Median codebase size 8,635 code lines (min 212, max 2,701,283) and 50 code files (p. 4). [V] Difficulty bins: Easy 28, Medium 143, Hard 29 (p. 31).
170	    45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filter for repositories that can produce a standalone executable, with compiled language as the heuristic. Repositories whose executable needs the internet are excluded; 18 networking tools are kept and tested over localhost (p. 3; p. 21). [I] How the 200 were chosen from the eligible pool (random, by stars, by build success) is not reported.
171	    46	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code at github.com/facebookresearch/ProgramBench, open-sourced (p. 1; p. 2).
172	    47	
173	    48	## 5. Experimental setup
174	    49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] mini-SWE-agent (bash-only minimal scaffold), vendor-default hyperparameters, 20 CPUs and 60 GB RAM per container, 1,000-step and 6-hour limits (p. 5), 3-minute per-action timeout, no cost limit, outputs truncated at 10,000 characters (p. 32). [V] Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 with Rust 1.92.0, Python 3.12, Go 1.21.0, a C/C++ toolchain and tmux for TUIs (p. 16). [V] Binary test assets that models cannot easily generate (images, audio, custom formats) are provided; standard text formats are not (p. 21; p. 22). [V] Before evaluation, all files matching the hash of the original executable are removed, and git history is wiped (p. 18; p. 19).
175	    50	- Number of runs: [V] One run per model-task (1,800 runs, p. 10). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
176	    51	- Code availability: [A] public (p. 1).
177	    52	
178	    53	## 6. Evaluation metrics
179	    54	- % Resolved: share of tasks where all tests pass and no cheating is flagged; the primary metric (p. 5).
180	    55	- % Almost: share of tasks with ≥95% of tests passing (p. 6).
181	    56	- % Tests Passed: per-task pass fraction. The authors say it is "only meaningful for relative comparisons" and "does not reliably correlate with percentage of working functionality" (p. 5).
182	    57	- Test-suite quality: line coverage of the original binary versus native suites; dummy pass rate (share of tests that a trivially wrong program passes) (p. 7; p. 8).
183	    58	- Code structure (descriptive): lines of code, number of files, maximum directory depth, function count and average function length, compared with the reference, for runs passing ≥75% of tests (p. 8; p. 9).
184	    59	- Trajectory metrics: action types (read/write/probe/execute/git) classified by keyword matching; edit counts; share of code written in the single largest edit (p. 9; p. 10).
185	    60	- Cheating rate: majority vote of 9 LM judges (p. 6; p. 17).
186	    61	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests or confidence intervals. The paper reports Pearson correlations of pass rate with API calls (r = 0.27) and cost (r = 0.21) (p. 33) and Fleiss' κ for judge agreement (p. 17). [I] The statement that "test pass rates are significantly different between models" (p. 2) is not backed by any reported test.
187	    62	
188	    63	## 7. Key findings
189	    64	1. [V] No model resolves any task (0% resolved for all 9). Claude Opus 4.7 reaches ≥95% of tests on 3.0% of tasks, Opus 4.6 on 2.5%, Sonnet 4.6 on 1.6%, and all others on 0% (p. 6).

191	    66	3. [V] Across all runs, the median pass rate is 32%; about 18% of runs fall in the 0–5% bin, and fewer than 5% exceed 90% (p. 32). C/C++ tasks average 27.7%, against 38.5% for Rust and 38.4% for Go (p. 33).
192	    67	4. [V] Generated test suites average 79.7% line coverage (median 86.2%), against 56.8% (median 64.3%) for native suites, over 100 sampled repositories. Against 12 dedicated behavioural/integration suites, coverage is 62.16% versus 66.11% (p. 7; p. 8).
193	    68	5. [V] The assertion linter cut the mean dummy pass rate from 18.5% to 3.7%, and the stricter tests were 20–30 percentage points harder to pass without changing the model ranking (p. 8; p. 23).
194	    69	6. [V] Models chose the reference language in exactly 50% of runs. Python was the most common choice overall (36% of 1,800 runs) (p. 8).
195	    70	7. [V] Among 207 runs passing ≥75% of tests (88 tasks), model code had a median of 1,173 lines against 3,068 for the reference, 3 files against 15, and maximum directory depth 1 against 2. 60% of solutions had 1–3 code files, and 67% were shallower than the reference (p. 9).
196	    71	8. [V] Models write 10–29% as many functions as the reference, and their functions are longer (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro 1.62x, Sonnet 4.6 1.46x, GPT 5.4 1.08x average length) (p. 8; p. 9).
197	    72	9. [V] Development styles differ widely. Sonnet 4.6 issues a median of 868 commands per task, GPT 5.4 17 (p. 9). GPT 5.4 writes nearly all its code in one turn and makes 1.2 file modifications per trajectory on average, with 39.5% of trajectories making none (p. 10; p. 11). Probing the executable is the second-largest action category, at 22.6–34.1% of turns (p. 10).
198	    73	10. [V] More turns or money do not reliably help: per-run correlation with pass rate is r = 0.27 for API calls and r = 0.21 for cost, driven mostly by between-model differences (p. 33).
199	    74	11. [V] Forcing a different implementation language lowered Opus 4.7 (−8.0%) and Opus 4.6 (−3.5%) but raised each GPT model by 4.2%; the share of Python rose to 51% (p. 6; p. 7).
200	    75	12. [V] With internet access, 20–36% of tasks were flagged as cheating for the three stronger models tested (1% for GPT 5 mini), mostly source-code lookup (79–95% of flags). Judges disagreed on many tasks, with pooled Fleiss' κ = 0.57 over 786 tasks (p. 6; p. 7; p. 17).

202	    77	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
203	    78	- [A] A finite test suite under-approximates the executable's full specification, so evaluation is a "lower bound" on correctness: passing solutions may still differ on untested inputs (p. 12; p. 3).
204	    79	- [A] Only input-output equivalence is tested. Non-functional properties (speed, memory, disk footprint) are not, so a passing solution could be far slower or more resource-hungry (p. 12).
205	    80	- [A] Only a single-agent baseline is evaluated; multi-agent and human-in-the-loop settings are left for future work (p. 12).
206	    81	- [A] Distinguishing meaningful behaviour from implementation artefacts is subjective. The gold executable is treated as the complete specification, and 5 tasks are at risk of implementation-dependent output (p. 26).
207	    82	- [A] No formal human study of feasibility; solvability is argued theoretically (Church–Turing) and from the observable, deterministic tests (p. 20).
208	    83	- [A] Cheating detection with LM judges is unreliable, so internet access is blocked by default (p. 6; p. 19).
209	    84	
210	    85	## 9. Limitations we identified
211	    86	- [I] Possible test-oracle bias. The test-writing agent had full access to the source code (p. 21) and used Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p. 3). The behaviours it chose to test may favour what a source reader finds salient, and same-family models (Claude) top the leaderboard (p. 31). The paper does not test for this.
212	    87	- [I] "Agent-driven fuzzing" (p. 1) overstates the method. The tests are LLM-written, coverage-guided pytest cases (p. 3; p. 23), not randomised input fuzzing. Coverage is high, but semantic coverage of edge cases is unknown.
213	    88	- [I] Contamination is only partly controlled. No-internet stops lookup, not memory. Many targets (FFmpeg, SQLite, jq, ripgrep) are famous and widely present in training data, and models can identify the program from `--help` output (p. 17). The different-language ablation (p. 5; p. 6) is the only memorisation probe, and its mixed results do not settle the question.
214	    89	- [I] Code-quality evidence is thin. Only size and structure statistics are reported (LoC, files, depth, function count and length) (p. 9), with no maintainability index, smells, duplication, tests, documentation or readability. These are computed only on runs passing ≥75% of tests, a selected subset, and are confounded by language changes: Python rewrites of C code are naturally shorter (p. 35). "Monolithic" is shown, but whether it is worse for maintenance is not measured.
215	    90	- [I] Single run per model-task (p. 10) with vendor-default sampling (p. 5), so run-to-run variance is unknown. Differences between closely ranked models (e.g. Opus 4.6 52.0% vs Opus 4.7 51.2%, p. 31) cannot be separated from noise.

217	    92	  - 1,800 runs (p. 10) vs 1,788 runs (p. 32);
218	    93	  - median tests per task 770 (p. 4) vs 750 (p. 23);
219	    94	  - the Fig. 12 boxplot shows Sonnet 42% and Gemini 51%, the text says 44% and 53%, and the caption says GPT 5.4 writes "a median of 96%" while the text says 100% (p. 10);
220	    95	  - "best model" is Opus 4.7 by % almost (p. 6), but Opus 4.6 has the higher mean pass rate (p. 31).
221	    96	  
222	    97	  None changes the conclusions, but they lower confidence in exact figures.
223	    98	- [I] The main metric (% resolved) is all-or-nothing and saturates at 0% for every model (p. 6), so it cannot rank models; the paper relies on the softer metric that it itself says is only relative (p. 5).

227	   102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: separate build and inference containers, execute-only binary, wiped git history, no internet, hash-based removal of the original binary (p. 18; p. 19). [I] Remaining threats: pretraining memory of famous programs; test generation by a same-family model with source access; the provided test assets may hint at tested behaviours (p. 21).
228	   103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Compiled-language CLI/TUI programs; a minimal single-agent scaffold, unlike practitioners' vibe-coding tools with rich IDE context and human steering (p. 5; p. 12).
229	   104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Behavioural equivalence on observable stdout/stderr/exit codes/files is a strong operational definition of functional fidelity for CLIs.
